title: What Happened to Art Criticism? by elkins, james Critical Mess: Art Critics on the State of Their Practice edited by rubinstein, raphael
abstract: Contemporary art critics appear to agree that their field faces deep problems. They are concerned, for one thing, about cutbacks in mainstream media coverage of visual art. J. J. Charlesworth in Critical Mess: Art Critics on the State of Their Practice laments the general “dumbing down” of the media, expressing concerns that public discourse on intellectual topics in general has become a “black hole” (p. 77). Ironically, as James Elkins notes, the problem is not that art criticism is itself dead or dying. It exists—but nobody reads it. Criticism is not archived or cataloged, and no one takes seriously the articles solicited by galleries for coffee table books. Elkins and various authors in Raphael Rubinstein's anthology speculate about why we are in this mess and what, if anything, can be done about it. Perhaps art writers themselves are at fault. Katy Siegel in Rubinstein alludes to “the crummy state of writing about art” (p. 43). Or perhaps today's art critics are not well trained—Rubinstein quotes painter John Currin's complaint that the culture around painting is “dead” (p. 35). Perhaps the crisis is symptomatic of the larger mess that is the contemporary artworld, where curators and gallery owners hijack the latest art school whizzes and hype their work at fairs like Art Basel Miami Beach, bypassing critics who subsequently bemoan the dominance of crass market forces. Rubinstein notes that the artworld has become so multiple and changing that it is difficult for critics to discern meaningful patterns. Much contemporary visual art is not just esoteric, but also, he fears, “derivative and dreary” (p. 34). Why is criticism needed at all? Rubinstein rightly points out that we think of art criticism as necessary in a different sense from, say, wine reviewing. Much as we might enjoy both art and wine, there is some deeper significance to art, which has a “substantial effect” on society and history (p. vii). Criticism should have something to say about this deeper significance. Further, it can ideally involve a productive interaction with artists. Nancy Princenthal writes, “What's missing is a notion of criticism as substantive and active dialogue with working artists” (p. 88). The contrast between art and wine criticism is telling, but the analysis in these books of how art critics can get at the deeper significance of their subject matter is limited by the fact that they see themselves as stuck in a dilemma: art critics must either rely on their “eye” or taste to pronounce value judgments or draw upon some theory of art to provide more analytical accounts of art's meaning and function. The former option renders critical opinions purely subjective, hence not much better than wine reviews. But the latter option founders, allegedly, because there are now no workable theories of art. Strangely, Clement Greenberg, whose influence appears to be both envied and despised, adopted both options, buying into a formalist theory of art that allegedly justified his reliance on his own “eye” to issue grand pronouncements of value. The dilemma as diagnosed here seems to me to be specious. First, there are other accounts of valuation besides the alternative between taste and big‐picture theory. The idea of “theory” invoked here is fuzzy and elusive. Discussions of evaluation in philosophy might have been helpful, such as Kendall Walton's notion of categories of art, which has been adapted and applied to develop ideas of genre‐based film criticism by film theorist Noël Carroll. This approach avoids the need for some one all‐encompassing theory of art. Furthermore, these books do not include any actual arguments that a “big theory” of art is no longer possible. Rubinstein complains in his essay “A Quiet Crisis” that critics today mainly see their job as description. “This has been a period of interpretation rather than judgment, which is no doubt why the philosophically inclined Arthur C. Danto has been the most widely read and cited critic of the last decade or so” (p. 33). Rubinstein misses the point that Danto has proposed a “big theory” of art, one that just so happens to be centered on the role of interpretation. For Danto, art is the presentation within certain artworld circumstances of an object under an interpretation. Critics need to discern the idea behind the art object and then assess how well the object embodies it. Given this view of the project, evaluation is not a priority, but neither is it ignored. In “The Fly in the Fly Bottle: The Explanation and Critical Judgment of Works of Art,” Danto says that since he chooses to write only on work that is already established, there is little need to go beyond discussing meaning and significance. As he has explained elsewhere: “My feeling is that critics have to learn to describe what they are looking at, meaning—learning to determine which parts of the object embody which parts of the meaning, after which there is not a lot to say by way of pronouncing value judgments” (“Ontology, Criticism, and the Riddle of Art versus Non‐Art in The Transfiguration of the Commonplace,”Contemporary Aesthetics 6 [2008] at http://www.contempaesthetics.org/newvolume/pages/article.php?articleID=505). Elkins appears similarly trapped by the false dichotomy between the critic's use of an eye in “mere” connoisseurship and adversion to some no‐longer‐plausible “big theory” of art as the basis for critical assessment. His example of the first option is critic Jerry Saltz, who takes stands but has no theory. Like Greenberg, Saltz considers personal vision crucial. Saltz writes, “Having an eye in criticism is as important as having an ear in music. It means discerning the original from the derivative, the inspired from the smart, the remarkable from the common… . Dishearteningly, many critics have ideas but no eye” (pp. 21–22 in Rubinstein). The problem Elkins has with this is that since Saltz cannot draw on any theory to back up his assessments, they wind up seeming arbitrary and idiosyncratic. But Elkins sees the only alternative as writing from some theory that itself cannot be defended. On this horn of the dilemma he locates Michael Fried, who does base assessments on his theory of art but cannot defend his theory, which is simply one that he finds himself accepting. This leaves Fried (and us) without an actual argument for the kinds of art he favors. Elkins leaves it unclear what it would mean to defend a theory of art. He advances a bizarre argument that theories of art that are new enough to cope with the latest work will not have any justification due to lacking a reception history, whereas the older, better justified theories will prove outmoded in application to the latest work. What, then, are critics to do? Elkins urges them to offer ambitious judgment based on knowledge of all of the relevant theories and literature and reflection upon judgment itself. Their criticism should be important enough to count as art history. As an example, he praises a piece by Peter Schjeldahl writing about Surrealism in a short review that is especially insightful. One writer who offers an approach to evaluation is Thomas McEvilley in his article in Critical Mess (“The Tomb of the Zombie,” reconstructed from a 1994 lecture). Any endorsement of critical judgment from McEvilley is surprising given his view that modernism in art (and art criticism) involved “fetishization of value judgments.” With Greenberg clearly in his sights he cautions, “If we want the rest of the cultural world to even begin to take our discourse seriously, we’ve got to demystify it from all of this insane romantic priestly power‐tripping” (p. 19). For McEvilley, since postmodernism rejects absolutes including universal value judgments, critics today can at best issue only judgments in which they acknowledge personal conditions and limitations on these judgments. He argues they can do this by relying not upon some big‐picture theory of art but on more local accounts of art's function and role in culture. McEvilley also makes a point that I believe reveals a serious limitation of the Rubinstein anthology. As Rubinstein admits in the introduction, it is “unforgiveably [sic] New‐York centric” (p. ii). He calls for someone with greater expertise to organize a companion volume with a global focus. As far back as 1994, McEvilley was urging more attention to art in the Third World. He reports that after his travels to other countries, the art scene back home in New York seemed flat and lifeless—perhaps too tainted by vagaries of art school and gallery‐market trends. I would not quarrel with the recommendation to adopt a more global focus, but both writers sidestep problems facing art critical writing in the United States. By comparison to film criticism, say, critics writing today in America must grapple with a lack of general public access to the art most art journals and critics focus on, that found in New York galleries. Michael Duncan does comment on this caustically, in his essay in Critical Mess, “The true provincialism of today's art institutions is their notion of globalism, one defined by an arbitrary A‐list of thirty international artists most of whom now live in New York or London” (p. 113). If art critics really wish to work in dialogue with working artists, as Princenthal envisages, they must do so on local levels in regional arts centers. This is a problem simply not addressed in these books. Eleanor Heartney mentions the possible role of the blogosphere in this enterprise, but dismisses it as a “Wild West” full of “unregulated voices” with no way to discern truth from falsehood (p. 105). Heartney's skepticism seems too hasty, given that in various cultural and intellectual spheres, certain blogs have in fact emerged as influential, widely read, and well respected. I see no reason why this could not happen in the field of art criticism. Indeed, the possibility has already received some serious consideration with the essay by Peter Plagens in Art in America, “Report from the Blogosphere: The New Grass Roots” (November 2007, pp. 61–69). The article, appropriately enough, took the form of an e‐mailed roundtable, in which Plagens interviewed five prominent art bloggers across the country about the purpose and nature of their blogs.

title: An Interview With Jon Cattapan
abstract: In The City Submerged the striking narratives of Cattapan's earlier Melbourne paintings are fragmented and set adrift, becoming tiny shards of archaeological evidence with no clear solution, no beginning, middle or end. Luminous blue green surfaces dissolve into pools of submarine light in these paintings; here there is no grounding in shadows, or alley-ways, only the flickering distortions of looking into water, whose depth is unknowable. The movement in the painting is continuous as a work in a state of flux, and within and across its shiny surfaces. Deborah Clarke "The Lost World a Tale of Two Cities" Dauber: As you are aware the theme for this edition of M/C reviews is COLOUR. When this theme was chosen your name and your paintings immediately sprang to mind. With regard to Australian painting today one could equate the name Cattapan with two things colour and the modern city or perhaps the city as a text for modernity? Whilst suggesting that your use of colour, and your conception of the city are dualities, there is a paradoxical quality about your use of colour. Would it be fair to say that the luxurious quality of the colour; "the luminous blue green surfaces, these pools of submarine light" invest your paintings with a quality of the magical or phantasmagorical? Cattapan: From about 1986 I became increasingly interested in nocturnal light and how to represent it. My cities are always places that occupy that nocturnal space. I see the quality of those blue -green works of mine as being very fugitive. The colouration is meant to evoke a kind of drifting. I've always been interested in Surrealism and in my own works there was for a time a kind of dream - tableau that the actions unfolded upon, but in particular it was the writings of louis Aragon that struck a chord for me. In his book 'The Paris Peasant' he speaks of drifting around Paris by night and coming across its urban markers as though they were magical hallucinations. I guess in part I tried to transpose those sentiments into a colour sense. Those deep blues and greens offer a sense of that drifting - of the fugitive - of the twilight - of being there but not there. Dauber: In 1989 you are quoted as saying that your work was about two things "a search for your own artistic identity" and " making a statement on the "human urban condition". However in these depictions of the city you seemed more concerned to elucidate the destructive elements of urban dwelling, alienation, isolation and impotence. As "notes" or as a "visual diary" were these works perhaps more intensely personal? Cattapan: During the late eighties and early nineties I made a lot of my work on paper. Almost all of it is diaristic in the sense that each drawing marks an impression of a place or time or mood - they are strongly autobiographical and yet they also mark the mood of the times and of course of urban situations. Dauber: You have lived and worked in some of the great cities of the world. In light of the recent catastrophic events in New York to figure the city as lost, or drowned, would now seem to be prophetic. In the City Submerged series of paintings you have created a great sense of ambiguity through a sense of play with the term "submerged". Like the lost city of Atlantis, your metaphorical blue-green city is at once covered, submerged and unknowable. Yet, your paintings simultaneously uncover the spectacle of the modern city. This seems to signify a re-enchantment with the city, which could perhaps be falsely interpreted as being opposed to your earlier paintings? Cattapan: You see the thing that's interesting about painting is that paradoxes over a longer period of time become part of the continuity of process. There has always been this love-hate representation in my work. So at times these cities of mine have looked almost apocalyptic and at other times they figure largely as spectacles of competing information (I'm thinking here of the 'datascapes' from '92 onwards). For the last couple of years I've moved back into narrative mode as a counterpoint - demonstrations, protest, sundry calamities - these too are part of our cities. They are weird barometers for our times. Jon Cattapan, detail from Veil (Big Economy Hype) 1994 Collection: Wollongong City Gallery Dauber: Could you tell us something of the way in which you create these paintings? You have utilized both the technology of the computer, and the more artistic concepts of the "brush" and "a la main". Cattapan: The large cityscape/datascape paintings are created by scanning photographs of various places to create a generic city. This is an important point - my cities are like electronic collages and these become my working drawings. The paintings always start as an abstract space where the main thing is colour and light. Over the top of this expressive underlay I paint carefully reproduced marks that from a distance give the impression of a city by night - always from a panoptic view. There is something curious in the translation, in that the hand made mark becomes highly subjective as an interpretive tool, and therefore much as I might try to simply replicate the collage, what results is a painterly colouration and discrete mark-making process of overlays that speaks about painting itself. Dauber: Your paintings are full of light - the winking lights of the city at night and the auratic light which comes from some underground source. It has been suggested that your paintings create a virtual reality and that the light which is shed is that of the pixel. Does this somehow situate the metropolis and within a global context, or does it elaborate the complexities of the interconnectedness of cities and the people within them? Could you elaborate this point? Cattapan: There is no doubt in my mind that the urban condition is at once local and global. The works are a response to an information saturated world and they seek to represent that, but they also tell stories of local environment, albeit in a sometimes very abstract way. Over the last couple of years the more narratively inclined works of city gatherings demonstrate again after a long absence my need to tell local stories - but they become global. These groupings of figures set against dissolving cityscapes now have a sad ring to them. Jon Cattapan, detail from Dissolve (there but not there) 1991 Dauber: Yes, the blue-green paintings are soft and seductive, but they also have an unavoidable edge of pathos which seems inherent in the colour blue, could you tell us something of the red paintings which seem to signal a change in mood or experience? Cattapan: Those deeply saturated works came directly out of the experience of going to India in 1996. Whereas blue is deeply reflective, red for me is about life energy. The 'red' works actually began whilst I was in India as a group of watercolours that I made in collaboration with the Indian artist, Surendran Nair. Dauber: This is very interesting because most people would associate energy and life with the concept of the city yet in many ways your blue paintings convey a sense of stillness, which I believe gives them their amazing reflective quality. Your work has often been compared with that of Whistler. Like you, Whistler had a fascination with the city which conveyed its mythic qualities. Many artists have endeavored to convey a lived experience of the city and its relationship with modernity. As "watchers" or spectators they have been concerned to transmit their experience of the city, its colour, and its diversity as a counterpoint to the rationality of the "concept city" which was supposedly ultimately manageable. The flanneur combined the passionate wonder of childhood with the analytic sophistication of the man of the world as he read the signs and impressions of "the outward show of life" of the city. Whilst you too, could be considered to be the 'flanneur", your work seems to lack this "outward show of life", the hustle and bustle of the city, the crowded plaza's, the presence of people, the "colour of the city"? Cattapan: You've ended on an interesting note and I think the best way to respond is to speak of a specific experience. When I went to live in New York at the end of 1989 I was convinced that by moving to a much larger urban environment I would be able to invest my work with some of those outward signs of a super metropolis. In fact the reverse occurred - a kind of numbness set in from the overactive lifestyle and overload of information. At the street level the 'narrative' conveyed a clear poetry and rationale which I felt was far bigger than my work. It was not as easy to mythologise the events on those streets as it was to mythologise St.Kilda. So instinctively, I began to 'bury' the narrative and focused instead on a more reflective psychological space through colour. I wanted to in effect hose down the babble - maybe I was a little melancholy. Walking around those oily dark deserted streets of Williamsburg by night reinforced all that. It led me bit by bit towards this idea of 'The City Submerged', which in turn gave way to the spectacle of shifting layers of light/data in the cityscapes from 92 onwards. I never thought of my works as simply celebrating the city, there is always a darker side to them, an ambiguity. Maybe that's why there's no hustle bustle, what you get instead is a kind of crackling uncertainty. I've painted the nocturnal city and its attendant information gathering connections as a metaphor for how our society is unfolding. References Clarke, Deborah. 'The Lost World A Tale of Two Cities. Jon Cattapan'. Art and Australia 33 (1996): 512-517. Friedburg, Anne. Window Shopping : Cinema and the Postmodern. Berkeley, Calif.: Uni

title: The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte (1891) by Claude Monet (1840–1926)
abstract: When does Modern Art begin? There's no simple answer. Historians who take the long view might look to the Italian Renaissance and the discovery of single-point perspective, proper proportion and correct anatomical detail. Or consider the year 1800, when a preternatural foreshadowing of our present age can be discerned in the severely objective vision of David and the proto-surrealism of Blake and Goya. Social historians look to the rise of the modern city, urbanism, the isolation of the individual, and industrialization as hallmarks of the Modern Age. For these reasons, among many others, art historians and theoreticians believe that Edouard Manet was the first modern artist and 1863 the critical year when he sent for exhibition the Dejeuner and the Olympia to the Salon, those two marvelous paintings bristling with psychological implication for the viewer and the first attempt in the West, by way of the Japanese woodcut, to flatten Renaissance perspective. But the public cares little for such theoretical discourse and almost everyone today knows that Impressionism was the first organized art movement of the modern era and that Claude Monet was its leading artist. Indeed, even Manet, the pater familias of the French Impressionists, was heavily influenced by his young friends in the last phase of his career. In the Post-Impressionist generation that followed, Paul Cezanne liked to say that Monet “was only an eye, but what an eye” as if his stylistic predecessor had never used his brain. As we shall see, Monet's intuition served him well and he lived long enough to make a number of important contributions to modern and contemporary art. Today, when any exhibition of Impressionist masters brings in throngs of viewers, and the paintings bring many millions of dollars at auction, it is difficult to remember how reviled Monet was during much of his lifetime, harder still to accept the truly revolutionary nature of his work. But Monet's stature in art history compares favorably with his popularity. In his emphasis on the impression, the stroke, the contrast of colors, and the consistency with which he was often the first to make an advance, and to take it to its most logical and radical conclusion, Monet was truly “the exemplary Impressionist.”1 Claude Monet was born in Paris on the 14th of November, 1840; he showed no interest in inheriting his father's wholesale grocery store, drew caricatures of his classmates and by the age of 15 was receiving commissions for paintings. It was in 1856 that he met Eugene Boudin in Le Havre, a painter obsessed by the notion of painting outdoors (en plein air); in his maturity, Monet systematized this interest and painted the same subject over and over in all varieties of weather and lighting conditions. In this way, the magnificent series of Haystacks, Poplars, Rouen Cathedrals, Houses of Parliament, and Water Lilies were born. Based on recent developments in color theory, Monet and his friends became interested in an accurate, objective and scientific depiction of the atmosphere or light through which objects were seen at different times of day and at different seasons. Monet was one of the first artists in history to take such an approach and his serial investigation of a fixed form under varying conditions became a central tenet of modern art; his example influenced Cezanne's still life compositions and views of Mont St. Victoire, the still lives of Picasso and Braque, the abstract Homages to the Square by Josef Albers, the Black Paintings and Protractors of Frank Stella, and the Incomplete Cubes of Sol LeWitt. It is interesting to note that Monet's experiments in serial images began after the 8th and final Impressionist group exhibition in 1886, a time when the movement seemed to have come to an end, the group dispersed and Monet was criticized by Degas as a mere decorator.2 As a colorist, Monet employed a broken brushstroke technique in which small patches of intense color were placed side-by-side (without mixing) in order to pump up the chromatic impact of his compositions. He usually chose colors that were complements on the color wheel (eg, red/green, yellow/violet, blue/orange) and used them at a pitch that would cause visual vibrations. His “objective” or scientific study of his subjects often gave way to his interest in color (Impressionism) and the palette of reds, greens, blues and violets that he favored. His color sense influenced Gauguin, van Gogh and Matisse. Monet never stopped experimenting and lived long enough into the 20th century that he began to worry about becoming an old fogey, an artist who had been superseded by the Fauvism of Matisse and the Cubism of Picasso and Braque. So, while his corneal opacities worsened, Monet began to artificially sculpt the waters and gardens on his property in Giverny and allowed his canvases to become environmental in size and impact. Into these wall-size paintings, Monet inserted diaphanous and indistinct brushstrokes that almost completely vaporized the Water Lilies and their reflections. When the paintings of the 1920s were first installed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, their intense color, vigorous abstraction and landscape orientation greatly influenced the development of Abstract Expressionism. In this way, Monet achieved a sort of revenge on Cezanne and his immediate Modernist successors; Pollock and his colleagues would eventually destroy the abstract grid upon which Cubism was based. But the Poplar series, made by Monet in the Summer and Fall of 1891, contains within it the germ of the grid, that indispensible organizing principle of 20th century abstract art: the Cubism of Picasso and Braque, the Platonic world of Mondrian, the idealized Squares of Albers, the serial boxes of Judd and LeWitt. Of course, artists since the Renaissance have used the grid to “square-up” and transfer drawings to walls but only in the 20th century did the grid become the chief organizing principle and subject of paintings and sculptures. Although Monet would return to an implied grid in the etherealized façade of his later Rouen Cathedrals, paintings in which he employed a vertical plane to explore a vertical subject, the grid is most forcibly evident in the Poplars. Monet found his Poplar trees in a marsh along the banks of the Epte River, a few miles upstream from his home in Giverny where he created his famous gardens. The artist reached his floating studio, moored in the water, by a small boat in a nearby waterway; the trees were lined up in single file along the S-curve of the main part of the stream. He created 3 groups of paintings in all: in one, the towering poplars go off the top edge of the canvas, an effect seen in the present example from the Metropolitan Museum in New York. In another group, somewhat crowded, there are 7 trees and in the third, there are 3 or 4 trees without the severe cropping and en face orientation seen in the painting on our cover. The poplar series is the culmination of an 8-month period of study. At a certain point, Monet had to buy the rights to the trees because he had not finished painting them and could not risk having them cut down! When he was done he released the rights to a lumber merchant. In my opinion, The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte is the supreme achievement in the series. The 4 trees emerge from the riverbank with much of their foliage shorn or not yet in place; each trunk is perfectly replicated by its reflection in the river and each is placed equidistant from its neighbors. Indeed, the series of trunks begins and ends with the same amount of space from the right and left hand margins of an almost perfectly square canvas (32 1/4 × 32 1/8″). The 4 trees, the 4 reflections, the 5 columns of sky and water, and the horizontal riverbank, form an abstract grid. The tan and ochre trunks, the green leaves, and the riverbank grasses, are lit by a subtle sunset of reds and yellows, blues and pinks, their symmetrical reflections thrown into the water below. The rigidity of the grid is emphasized by the arbitrary amputation of the trees at the top of the canvas and the abbreviation of the reflections at its bottom. The presence of the grid in a typical Monet is made even more striking by his characteristic avoidance of outline and contour, his dissolution of line.1 Furthermore, unlike almost all the other paintings in the Poplar series, the trees are seen en face and not on a diagonal or from the side. This confrontational orientation, the flat grid-like presentation of the subject, not to mention the beautiful harmony of the colors, must account for the painting's powerful effect on the viewer and his visual system. Almost seventy years after Monet painted this scene, the symmetrical grid was ensconced in contemporary art and discovered to be one of the most efficient stimuli in eliciting cellular responses in the primary visual cortex of mammals. Before then, in one of the most beautifully titled and imaginative papers in the history of neurobiology, Jerry Lettvin and his colleagues at MIT demonstrated the excitatory response elicited by curvilinear shapes introduced into the receptive field of frog visual neurons3; the investigators hypothesized that such cells would act as “bug” detectors, allowing the frog to flick out its tongue at targeted prey. Based on this work, as well as Mountcastle's pioneering topographic studies of cellular responses in somatosensory cortex, Hubel and Wiesel began a series of experiments in the visual cortex of cats and spider monkeys that would win them the Nobel Prize.4 Sometimes “noise” boards with various rectilinear shapes, somewhat resembling late Kandinsky paintings or work by Franz Kline, were used to determine the general preferences of single cells in the retina, optic tract, lateral geniculate body and primary visual cortex of paralyzed animals facing a projection screen. Light bars of various orientations, from complete vertical to complete horizontal, were used to sharpen the preference of the cell and determine the size of its receptive field. Inputs of several of these “simple” cells were hypothesized to converge on a single “complex” or “hyper-complex” cell with the same orientation preference but larger receptive fields and a different pattern of surround inhibition and excitation.4 Some of the simple and complex cells were powerfully stimulated not just by a single bar moving across their receptive field but by a properly oriented grid of bars with a specific angular frequency, ie, a sine-wave grating similar to that seen in Monet's painting. Subsequent experiments in primates demonstrated the existence of multiple visual systems for shape, movement, and color, not to mention objects, numbers and faces, many of which systems would be optimally stimulated by the heightened properties of shape and color in a Monet painting such as The Four Poplars.5 Individual neurons in the visual system, as elsewhere in the brain, signal their excitation by a frequency code. In the case of stimuli with properties of angular or spatial frequency (ie, grids) or sounds with a particular auditory frequency (ie, pitch), the firing of neurons can directly reflect the spatial or temporal frequency of the stimulus.6 In fact, some mathematical treatments of neuronal output as a function of time (eg, an interspike interval histogram or ISIH) quite closely resemble the shape of the stimulus; the frequency of the peaks in the ISIH of a simple cell in area 17 of the monkey increases as the spatial frequency of a stimulating grid of light bars on the retina increases.7 Presumably this is just as true for a grid of poplar trees. The supposed simplification of art objects in the 20th century actually represents an intensification and isolation of the various component strategies that artists employ to excite the brain. Zeki has argued that artists are intuitive masters of neuropsychology. Calder's mobiles, the giant portraits of Chuck Close, the intense colors of Matisse and the spatial grids of Mondrian, Agnes Martin and Sol LeWitt all serve to maximally excite different visual pathways. In some respects, the progressive disentanglement of our many visual systems began with the beautiful colors and subtle insinuation of a modernist grid in The Four Poplars. Contra Cezanne, Monet was much more than a magnificent eye; he was a true revolutionary. The first of the impressionist painters to achieve success and the last to die, 40 years after his movement officially ended, Monet kept pushing his art decisively forward. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: COVER ESSAY
abstract: SEA-SEA (1970) BY GERHARD RICHTER (b. 1932) The invention of photography in 1837 changed the form and function of painting forever. No longer the optimal medium for portraiture, scientific documentation or for the production of a verisimilitude of nature and outer reality, painting was freed to become increasingly abstract, to become a medium like music or poetry, an explorer of psychological or philosophical truths and inner verities. The supposed advantages of photography, its portability, its scientific objectivity and its reproducibility, came with certain artistic losses: a physically flat surface, easily multiplied in endless copies, that cut the cord or autographic connection between the audience and the author of the work. In short, the small black and white photographs of the later nineteenth and early twentieth centuries did not seem to share “the aura” and uniqueness of a masterpiece created on canvas. To some degree, the endless multiplication and easy availability of images of Leonardo's Mona Lisa also damaged the magic of the original; one no longer needed to visit the Louvre in order to commune with La Giaconda but could easily turn to a magazine or newspaper. The power of the mass media and the world's drowning in a flood of images only became worse with the invention of moving pictures, the subject of Walter Benjamin's essential essay, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” (1936), the brilliant exegesis in which the concept of “aura” was first bruited and the fascistic use of mass media predicted. Benjamin also foresaw a time when everyone would become a writer rather than a reader (ie, the development of “blogs”) and all the arts would become “mass” in nature and somewhat debased.1 What he could not foresee was the invention of the hand-held video camera around 1970 and the use of computer programs to “edit” or fictionalize photography through colorization, massive enlargement and other types of manipulation. In a manner similar to the way in which painting and drawing were changed by photography, sculpture and installation have been jolted and altered by motion pictures, video and computer-generated effects. Paradoxically, the impact of these changes has been greatest on photography itself; a medium that once reveled in its differences from painting became, in the 1980s and 1990s, a substitute or “simulacrum” of painting, aping the coloristic effects and grand scale of the older medium, taking upon itself the functions of nineteenth century history painting and twentieth century surrealism and fantasy. Along the way, art photography lost its role in social documentation and much of its scientific reliability. The generation of German photographers trained in Dusseldorf by Bernd and Hilla Becher, Thomas Ruff, Candida Hofer, Thomas Struth and Andreas Gursky, as well as that American master of self-disguise Cindy Sherman, produced photographs that commented on painting by directly imitating its most classical (ie, non-tactile) effects, photographs that successfully competed for visual impact and dollars in the marketplace of ideas and artistic success. For the umpteenth time in the course of the 20th century, painting appeared to be well and truly “dead.”FIGURE: Caption not available.Into this debate on the role of photography in late Modernism and the relative importance of painting stepped Gerhard Richter (b. 1932), also once a professor in Dusseldorf, who has spent fifty years utilizing painting to comment on photography rather than the other way around. Richter has the ability to meld the technical virtuosity of a Vermeer with the conceptual brilliance of a Duchamp; in this way he has managed to recuperate all of the classical tropes of painting, its usefulness in scientific documentation, portraiture and history, its ability to fool the eye, the concept of the masterpiece and the uniqueness of the author while, at the same time, eschewing all evidence of emotion, and denying the possibility of a “signature style.” By signature style I mean all those elements of a picture like paint handling, color palette and range of subject matter, that make any authentic Monet or Rembrandt self-evidently look like a “Monet” or a “Rembrandt” whether or not the painting is signed. How and why has Richter done this? Is the chameleon-like appearance of his work simply a joke, a kind of braggadocio to prove that he can do anything he wants to do really well or a serious commentary on our largely image-mediated world? Are the cool surfaces of his paintings simply further evidence of his bloody-minded nature or are even paintings such as these susceptible to real emotions and philosophical inquiry? To begin with, Richter paints photographs, that is to say, photorealist paintings that look like photographs (he even smears his immaculate surfaces to give a hint of the optical blur produced by the lens), many of which are based on photographs he has taken or travel souvenirs and postcards or found snapshots in the meaning that Duchamp gave to his “readymade” objects. Further, Richter often paints on photographs thereby expunging the physical separation of the two media, the photographic ground contributing the representational (ie, figurative) component of the picture while his brushstrokes add the abstract portion. In Richter's hall of mirrors, it is possible to buy an original photograph he's recently made of a painting that he once painted, a painting originally based on a photograph taken or found by Richter. At times Richter has even painted wholly abstract paintings based on photographs of brushstrokes randomly made and smeared on specimen cards kept in his files and documented in his on-going project, Atlas.2 In this way and others, Richter eliminates the conceptual difference between photography and painting since all of his early work, whether wholly abstract or wholly figurative in nature is based on an image-mediated world (ie, photographs) rather than any actual experience of the real world. Richter believes in the essential equivalency of abstraction and representation; he has painted hundreds of works in each mode but rarely combines the two. His more recent abstractions have been “spontaneously” made but share the cool photographic surfaces of the earlier photo-based abstractions. His photorealist portraits and landscapes are clearly recognizable as “Richters,” so too his classic abstract paintings in acid reds, greens and blues, his color chart paintings made of random assortments of paint samples, his mirror paintings in which the viewer sees himself and his environment. In this way, Richter has put an end to the concept of the signature style and has helped inaugurate Post-Modernism, the pluralistic and self-referential artistic period in which we live. A Richter retrospective looks like a group show put on by a half-dozen emotionally cool geniuses from several different artistic schools; simply put, he is the most important painter in the contemporary world. Politics helped form him. He was fortunate to be born in Dresden, while it was still “in” East Germany; there he was forced to learn classical artistic skills in order to produce bland Soviet-style art. Like Picasso and Matisse before him, Richter draws like an angel and his color sense is acute. Eventually his repressive education would make him develop an artistic practice in which he might use his formidable talents. For a while the only work he could find was the painting of stage sets. Stultified by his environment, he escaped to the West in 1962 and, with his artistic partner Sigmar Polke (1943-2010), became greatly influenced by American Pop Art and Andy Warhol in particular. For a brief time, Richter and Polke formed one of the great artistic dyads, like Picasso and Braque, and laughingly invented a new movement called “Capitalist Realism,” a short-lived style in which paintings based on commercial products and ads were combined with a kind of “living sculpture” or performance art. As if the gallery functioned like a furniture showroom, Polke and Richter hung out on the couches all the time their pictures were shown. And Richter destroyed all of the art he had made prior to moving to the West. Almost all of his earliest surviving paintings are photorealist in nature and painted in gray tonalities, en grisaille, so as to better imitate their sources in black and white photographs. Richter invented a series of cardboard and plastic “combs” with which he could smear his perfectly made photographic copies and introduce the optical distortion of the camera lens thereby tipping off the viewer that the real subject of the painting was the physical photograph itself and not merely the object contained within it. Of course, not all photographic subjects are of equal weight; Richter is old enough to have lived through the Second World War and has close family members who belonged to the Nazi Party and served as German soldiers. One of his most famous early paintings is “Uncle Rudi” (1965), based on a family snapshot of his father's brother proudly posed and smiling in his Wehrmacht uniform. After painting a series of black and white mountains, Richter turned to the sea and produced a stunning group of canvases intended to function as seascapes (1969-1970). These are at once the most abstract and the most powerful seascapes painted since the nineteenth century, the majority of them greater than six feet on a side. They are composed of pure water and sky without evidence of ships, humans or animals. The even tonalities of white, gray and black compacted into clouds and waves above and below the horizon line increase the sense of brooding menace and produce an abstract effect like that of Rothko's exactly contemporaneous late paintings in which a single rectangle of dark color floats on either side of a horizontal line. Although all of these seascapes are beautiful and stupendous to behold, I believe that “Sea-Sea” (1970) is the most impressive of them all. The key to Richter's subterfuge is in the title, the two “seas”, and his trickery revealed in plate 194 of Atlas; the source for the painting is actually a photo-collage in which Richter has glued together the ocean from one snap to serve as the sea in his painting and the sea from another snap to serve as the sky.2 Before computer manipulated pictures became possible, Richter knew that the modern photograph could lie and so could one of his painted photographs. Of course, we want to see a stormy sky above a wave-swept sea. When visual input is inconclusive, the visual system adjusts the processing of current input on the basis of past experience; this effect can be demonstrated in both short-term and long-term situations.3 Our brains are hard-wired to make sense of the world based on incomplete information; it's a wonder that we are so often correct in our conclusions. The visual system, in particular, obeys the biological imperative to keep us safe in a world of environmental dangers and fleeing prey; its fleeting glimpses conveyed by the two optic nerves represent one third of the entire input (6 million afferent fibers) to the brain's CPU, and the brain must often complete the incomplete information it receives. Stimuli without a clear structure, like Rorschach inkblots, allow multiple interpretations, some of which depend on which visual field (ie, hemisphere) receives the information.4 Richter makes the processing of his image as difficult as possible by eliminating our expectation of a figure/ground relationship. Confronted by a visual image we seem to need a dominant shape or figure, with a definite contour, set against a background; the figure-ground relationship is one of the great discoveries of Gestalt psychology. In addition, we prefer figures that obey the gestalt law of Prägnanz, the tendency towards meaning, simplicity and completeness. In “Sea-Sea” there is uniformity above and below the horizon line with no definite figure, everything is “ground” and everything appears to be water. The hundreds of wavelets are too numerous for us to properly analyze; furthermore we expect them to move. Matisse commented that “movement thus understood corresponds to nothing in nature: when we capture it by surprise in a snapshot, the resulting image reminds us of nothing that we have seen”5; Richter has painted just such a snapshot. Spatial ambiguity in such a picture is further increased when color effects are removed and the eye must depend on the gray scale alone. In the Renaissance, wall paintings of statues situated in architectural niches were often painted in whites and grays so as to better create the illusion of shallow depth when deep shadows were not realistic or physically possible. The spatial recession in Richter's painting is similarly shallow and ambiguous; this image of “sky” and ocean hovers in its uniform treatment of “object” between the real world and the empyrean of an abstract universe, between something we know and something we're not quite sure of, like the photograph real and not-real, like the modern painting too, an object in our world and yet not completely of it. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: Only a Promise of Happiness: The Place of Beauty in a World of Artby nehamas, alexander
abstract: Alexander Nehamas's new monograph offers a contemporary defense of the Platonic conception of beauty as the object of love. In the historical trajectory he traces, disinterestedness theorists such as Immanuel Kant and Arthur Schopenhauer and twentieth‐century formalists such as Clive Bell and Clement Greenberg separated beauty from passion. Distinguishing aesthetic value from beauty, appearance, and pleasure, modernism, in Nehamas's narrative, cordoned off the difficult meanings proper to art from the prosaic dispensations of ordinary life. Beauty was banned from art, and relegated to the everyday. Fearful of beauty's social powerlessness and moral ambivalence, philosophy drove it into the arms of biology, psychology, fashion, advertising, and marketing. By returning desire to the beautiful, Nehamas affirms the pervasive and complex quotidian significance of beauty, whether in the form of persons, things, or artworks, of which philosophy has lost sight. His understanding of beauty as a product of love squarely situates it at the core of subjectivity. Human beings have a capacity for love, which can attach to anything, and a need to be affected by beauty. Since love finds beauty—Nehamas considers love of the ugly paradoxical—and beauty inspires love, beauty's seductions and challenges lie at the heart of the ways life matters to us. Only a Promise of Happiness: The Place of Beauty in a World of Art locates beauty's origins in the subject's loving relations to the world, and thereby provides an illuminating explanation of beauty's broad existential scope and import. The book contributes a significant chapter to the debates on beauty that have bloomed across the disciplines over the past decade, comprising, among other things, book‐length treatments by Elaine Scarry and Arthur C. Danto, an anthology by Peg Brand, and issues of Art Journal (2004) and Feminist Theory (2006). Nehamas's beauty does not speak with Kant's universal voice. It shares its temporality with that of our evolving loves, which, varying from transitory flames to abiding affections, can deplete or expand. Though beauty is fundamentally tied to the good, it withholds any moral or existential guarantee: beauty, for Nehamas, issues only a promise of happiness. A beautiful thing promises to make your life better when it becomes part of it. Nothing else holds out the same promise, and there is no knowing where the desire the thing evokes will take you. Beauty is an inexhaustible source of significance because our love for it resists closure of the meaning of the object. Faced with the ever‐retreating satisfaction of our desire, we keep interpreting the beautiful object, impelled to find out what incites our love. Immersed in unpredictably morphing desires, we find our lives unfolding in unforeseen directions. The beautiful leaves us vulnerable. It demands a surrendering of self. Our involvement with beauty is “personal” (p. 85), but as we give ourselves over to the things we consider beautiful, hoping to discover what makes them so, we engage others: “the desire beauty provokes is essentially social: it literally does create a new society for it needs to be communicated to others and pursued in their company” (p. 77). Relaying to his readers the story of his own interaction with Manet's Olympia, which brings him in conversation with, among others, T. J. Clark and Griselda Pollock, creating a dialogue that now also extends to his own readership, Nehamas illustrates how beauty gives rise to small communities. The productivity of Nehamas's view finds expression in the many subsidiary points on which he rests his theory. He persuasively casts off the hold of aesthetic concepts over our understanding of aesthetic life, compellingly resists the philosophical preoccupation with aesthetic verdicts, provides helpful commentaries on the interminable nature of interpretation, perspicaciously lays out the parallels and differences between the beautiful and the attractive as well as the good‐looking, and offers crucial critiques of empirical experiments, especially of studies of our responses to pictures of facial characteristics. These, he indicates, fail to warrant conclusions as to the nature of our ordinary judgments of beauty. Ranging across a wide scope of media and artifacts and weaving together observations on Marcel Proust and Oscar Wilde with discussions of philosophers such as Mary Mothersill and Danto and critics such as Michael Fried and Dave Hickey, the argument articulates a fluently interdisciplinary sense of aesthetic methodology. The book's scene of loving communal exchange becomes the stage for an encounter between two of Nehamas's regular interlocutors: Friedrich Nietzsche is called upon to supplement the expansive Platonic passion for beauty with the concentrated power of style. Drawing on Nietzsche's vision of the single style, or a consistent taste that shapes the admirable character, Nehamas finds in originality and coherence of character and style the grounds for a person's individuality. Just as good taste, according to Nehamas, requires originality, beauty, like other aesthetic features, is unique to each object. No object shares its aesthetic properties with any other object from which it is distinguishable. In relation to the beautiful, the particularity of the lover of beauty matches then the particularity of the object: “To interpret is to try to see in things what is distinctly their own. That is in turn to see them in ways that are distinctly our own and, to the extent that they are ours alone, these ways of seeing turn out to be aesthetic features in their own right and have themselves a claim to beauty” (p. 132). Two points follow from this. One, by finding beauty, we can come to create it ourselves. Notably, we can initiate a new way of looking at the world. Two, we may become beautiful ourselves, as our distinctive character, style, sensibility, and taste inspire love in others. Nehamas's view of the particularity of beauty and its purveyor seals his Platonic picture of the developmental cycle that propels us toward a more “synoptic vision of the world” (p. 120). Contra to Plato, however, a division ensues between beauty and moral goodness. In Nehamas's account, moral values aspire to shared human qualities, while aesthetic values direct us toward difference and distinction. Accordingly, taste and virtue can stand in tension with one another. Nehamas clarifies beauty's affective and cognitive functioning while affirming also its social, cultural, and biological dimensions. He suggestively reframes certain aesthetic questions. However, he gives insufficient attention to several phenomena of which any account of beauty must take note. His analysis downplays the institutional pressures guiding our passions. Capitalist market cultures, regimes of consumption, and technological developments powerfully impact affective life. Social and economic hierarchies move us to love certain things over other things, sensitizing us to specific possibilities for love, while inhibiting other ones. Artistic and quotidian canons of taste exert a strong pull over aesthetic perception and affect. Toni Morrison's Pecola Breedlove in The Bluest Eye unqualifiedly loved the blue eyes of white girls, while loathing her own. The desires we feel for beautiful things and people reflect systemic patterns of social differentiation. Loving orientations to the world carry the marks of institutionalized modes of production, consumption, environmental exploitation, and aesthetic regulation, which partially shape our lifeworlds. Via their influence on desire, systemic social structures differentially impact the good that our loves introduce to our own and others' lives. Contra to what Nehamas might reply, such effects cannot be shuttled off to the realm of unknowability, moral uncertainty, and risk surrounding the beautiful. Our social positionings in terms of categories of difference and identity substantially control our access to a wide range of human goods. While there is a measure of unpredictability to the ways in which matters of class, race, and gender govern what a given individual can make of life's various promises, what desires the person will have, and what good can come of these desires, the pervasive effects of these factors have been well documented. Nehamas by and large ignores the institutional conditioning of desire. The result is a depoliticized picture of beauty's significance. The politics of love receive short shrift. This undermines the book's hold on the quotidian meanings of the beautiful. In sidestepping the institutional dimensions of our traffic with things beautiful, ugly, or indifferent, Nehamas also diminishes the moral demands beauty's promises and threats make on us. Resisting phenomena such as Pecola's love and hatred requires a forsaking of personality in advance of the encounter with specific beautiful objects. A selective distancing from desire is needed to counteract structural influences on our engagement with beautiful things, people, and artworks. Through a careful critical suspension of our feelings of love, indifference, and disaffection, we can orient our desires to beauties that elude pre‐scripted paths of affiliation. This is not to say that the emotional economy of the beautiful can be put to right by anything short of fundamental global transformations, but it is to identify a moment of agency in our aesthetic attitudes. Regardless of how we take up the choices we face here, the theory of beauty should incorporate a critique of desire into its understanding of aesthetic subjectivity. The structural underpinnings of desire make their appearance also in the communities Nehamas sees taking shape around the love of beautiful objects. Absent a discussion of the terms of membership, it is hard to see what the value is of participation in such collectives. Communities centering around objects of aesthetic love, such as experimental cinema, hip‐hop, or surrealism, rest upon constitutive exclusions. In leaving unquestioned the qualifications for community membership, Nehamas's view projects a notion of aesthetic democracy and pluralism that is belied by the exclusions that arise in consequence of the differential and hierarchical social conditioning of desire and appreciation. Our loves are famously affected by needs and longings that are intractable to us. Idealization and fantasy, as the figure of Narcissus suggests, infuse our loving investment in the beautiful. Many of us enthusiastically tend to love objects and persons that mirror idealized images of ourselves to ourselves. Nehamas's conception of beauty's social dimension fails to avert the potentially narcissistic draw of the communal bonds he envisages. The emphasis on personal distinction and the good of the individual, rather than the good of an enlarged community, readily admits of a narcissistic involvement with the beautiful. This point presses again for a closer examination of the terms of engagement in the circles of affiliation encompassing the beautiful. Nehamas underscores the new that beauty promises to introduce to our lives. We hope to change as a result of our interaction with beautiful people and things. Beauty orients us to new desires, insights, people, and things. These forward‐looking elements of our relation to the beautiful, to my mind, also mark consumerism. Nehamas notes that the love of beauty includes a desire to possess the loved person or object. Yet, unlike the consumer, he insists, the lover wishes to be possessed by the loved object in turn, and welcomes the transformations this entails, trusting the object to awaken new desires (pp. 55–57). This idea does not quite capture the difference between consumerism and the pursuit of beauty, however. As consumers we often think of ourselves partially in terms of our purchases, and welcome the personal changes we hope will follow from this identification, including new desires. Part of the attraction of consumerism is that we will “become” what we wear and own. Nehamas uses the examples of friendship, amorous relationships, and his own love for Olympia, Proust, and other cultural productions to characterize the love of beauty more generally. Might the logic of consumption tell us something about quotidian beauty that these paradigms of love fail to capture? The separation of the love of beauty from consumption lends the former a false appearance of protection from critiques of the latter. Consumerism enters the love of beauty in a variety of forms: commodification of persons, a dynamic of obsolescence and replacement, possibilities for self‐stylization, and the paradoxical marketability of distinction. Our love of beautiful things, whether mass‐produced or unique, often reflects their ability to represent a type of personality or lifestyle rather than a distinctive character. Nehamas overestimates the particularity of the beauty we encounter in many objects and of our love for them. In this light it is worth considering his claim that we feel compelled to find out what it is about beautiful objects that makes them beautiful and causes them to stand out in our world (p. 131). Beautiful breads, teeth, voices, beads, doorknobs, rustling, and moss are not things I necessarily want to know more about, despite my love of them. This also goes for certain beautiful songs, dances, and paintings. Nehamas could rejoin that my engagement with these elements is not really so loving. But this would discount a great many of my everyday affiliations with persons, things, events, and artworks. Nehamas's argument attests to the existential import of our loving relations to beauty. However, he overemphasizes individual difference at the cost of structural influences on desire and thereby misconstrues the distinction between the values of aesthetics and morality. Ignoring the cultural terms and conditions that enable and undercut our relations to beauty, the book dismisses the ethics and politics of beauty in which we participate on a daily basis.

title: “First Surrealists Were Cavemen”: The American Abstract Artists and Their Appropriation of Prehistoric Rock Pictures in 1937
abstract: Previous articleNext article Free“First Surrealists Were Cavemen”: The American Abstract Artists and Their Appropriation of Prehistoric Rock Pictures in 1937Elke SeibertElke SeibertPDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreHow electrifying it must be to discover a world of new, hitherto unseen pictures! Scholars and artists have described their awe at encountering the extraordinary paintings of Altamira and Lascaux in rich prose, instilling in us the desire to hunt for other such discoveries.1But how does art affect art and how does one work of art influence another? In the following, I will argue for a causal relationship between the 1937 exhibition Prehistoric Rock Pictures in Europe and Africa shown at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and the new artistic directions evident in the work of certain New York artists immediately thereafter.2 The title for one review of this exhibition, “First Surrealists Were Cavemen,” expressed the unsettling, alien, mysterious, and provocative quality of these prehistoric paintings waiting to be discovered by American audiences (fig. 1).3 The title moreover illustrates the extent to which American art criticism continued to misunderstand surrealist artists and used the term surrealism in a pejorative manner.Fig. 1. “First Surrealists Were Cavemen.” Review of Prehistoric Rock Pictures in Europe and Africa at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, 28 April to 30 May 1937, Milwaukee Sentinel, 20 May 1937, 13.This essay traces how the group known as the American Abstract Artists (AAA) appropriated prehistoric paintings in the late 1930s. The term employed in the discourse on archaic artists and artistic concepts prior to 1937 was primitivism, a term due not least to John Graham’s System and Dialectics of Art as well as his essay “Primitive Art and Picasso,” both published in 1937 and influential to the AAA members.4 Within this discourse the art of the Ice Age was conspicuous not only on account of the previously unimagined timespan it traversed but also because of the magical discovery of incipient human creativity. The spatial dimensions of the cave, the three-dimensional surface of the rock walls, the effects of light and shadow, and the movement within the pictorial composition—all these struck a nerve with artists in New York.My thesis is that prehistoric cave pictures inspired the genesis of contemporary art, and, to my knowledge, I am the first to research the art of the AAA group within this context. This article is intended as a contribution to fill this gap and to frame the argument of a book-length project I am pursuing on this topic. Members of the AAA were forerunners of nonfigurative art, and they published widely regarded statements directed against the art establishment of their time, as a few examples will highlight in the following. I will be drawing on selected texts by Irving Sandler, now held in the special collections of the Getty Research Institute, as I seek to work through the role of these pioneering abstract artists. In my conclusion, and as an outlook, I will highlight this exhibition of copies of prehistoric cave paintings received at MoMA as an object for future research. This essay, along with my book project, is intended as a contribution to the historiography of American art history and to accentuate a lesser-known aspect of this great narrative.The AAA Group and Its NetworkThroughout the 1930s, members of the AAA group sought to distinguish their work from cubism, regionalism, and social realism in search of their own style. Though interested in advancing the technique of automatism, they also sought to maintain control of their pictorial means. Most of the AAA members were abstract or constructivist artists aligned with the School of Paris. During its foundational period around 1936, this loose group had no manifesto. It included as members Josef Albers, Rosalind Bengelsdorf, Ilya Bolotowsky, Harry Bowden, Byron Browne, Giorgio Cavallon, Burgoyne Diller, Werner Drewes, John Ferren, Suzy Frelinghuysen, Albert Gallatin, Gertrude Glass Greene and Balcomb Greene, Harry Holtzman, Carl Robert Holty, Ray Kaiser (the future Ray Eames), Paul Kelpe, Ibram Lassaw, Alice Mason, George McNeil, George Lovett Kingsland Morris, John Opper, Esphyr Slobodkina, Louis Schanker, David Smith, Albert Swinden, Rupert Turnbull, Vaclav Vytlacil, and Wilfrid Zogbaum, among others.5 Arshile Gorky and Willem De Kooning were close to the group, although they were not official members.Balcomb Greene, the long-standing chairperson of the AAA, recounted the group’s founding in the following terms:There was disagreement in the A.A.A. from the start. Holtzman and Gorky wanted A.A.A. to be an educational organization with classes. Holtzman sounded as if he wanted to be the teacher. Gorky wanted discipline like working in black, red and white. Gorky wanted no exhibitions and stormed out when he was voted down. The group had no general position on abstraction but would argue the point on individual paintings. There was a feeling that art had its roots in nature (Hofmann position).6Some still were students of Hans Hofmann at the Art Students League of New York and then at his private academy on Fifth Avenue, and had not yet established themselves.7 Hofmann influenced their art and introduced them to Piet Mondrian, who from October 1940 onward regularly participated in the group’s meetings. Members of the geometric and lyrical abstract movements also joined the AAA group, but the number of Mondrian adherents predominated. Contemporary artists in the mid-1930s regarded archaic art to be part of nature in general, while all American painters at the time were inspired by nature. In an oral history conversation recorded with Irving Sandler, Vytlacil noted: “Geometric abstraction—people just experimented with it—nothing doctrinaire—Idealism was in the attempt to create a new form…. we felt … The picture must be an object complete in itself … definitely interested in pictorial structure.”8 The AAA was the first such group to turn its back on earlier styles and embrace abstract art, though whether it could be called a homogeneous group or indeed felt it truly belonged is open to debate. Their statutes, set out in 1936, state: “We believe that a new art form has been established which is definite enough in character to demand this unified effort.”9During the group’s seminal and innovative years from 1936 to 1940, they could study works by European avant-garde artists at exhibitions organized by the Pierre Matisse Gallery, by Gallatin’s Museum of Living Art, and at MoMA. But what was the origin of the expressivity in the works of the AAA members? Have we overlooked a source for their inspiration? Certainly, New York artists closely observed important developments in Europe. But they also continued to seek a distinct, independent path, as their texts make clear and as this essay argues.There was a fruitful mobility and exchange of ideas between Paris and New York. Pablo Picasso, who undoubtedly drew inspiration from Magdalenian cave paintings in France, served as one model for the lyrical abstract painters. This was an open secret, not least as Picasso’s mural-sized painting Guernica, with its archaic references to bull motifs, impressed the crowds attending the Exposition Internationale in Paris in 1937.10 Moreover, the artificial cave devised by the prehistorian Henri Breuil, complete with copies of prehistoric cave paintings and artifacts, which was also accessible on the grounds of the exposition, gave attendees at the fair the remarkable opportunity of directly comparing the two works with each other. Breuil and Hugo Obermaier’s 1935 publication, The Cave of Altamira at Santillana del Mar, Spain, widely disseminated the transcriptions or reproductions of these impressive and picturesque animal depictions.11 The French journal Cahier d’Art, which juxtaposed the avant-garde paintings of André Masson, Joan Miró, or Paul Klee with these recently discovered prehistoric paintings, further laid the groundwork for this reception. Constructing the concept of the prehistoric presupposed a linear chronological development that in turned allowed for the isolation of sedimentation, or a time capsule. This in turn became a projection space for visual artists on both sides of the Atlantic and shaped the discourse of the era. However, it was not just the desire for an unblemished prehistory of humankind that was driving the debate surrounding the concept of the prehistoric. It was also the search for a primal creativity.Into this pulsating atmosphere with its sense of departure for new vistas, the AAA inserted itself as an alliance dedicated to establishing an exhibition space for nonfigurative art and sustaining the hopes of its members during the Great Depression. Most of them worked for the Federal Art Project (FAP), which frequently established the connections between the artists and accelerated the group’s consolidation. Both their daily collaboration and their work for the FAP’s Mural Division, for instance, under Burgoyne Diller, a key founding figure of the AAA, established friendships and encouraged the circulation of artistic opinions. In 1937, Gorky took inspiration from Stuart Davis’s large-scale paintings and Fernand Léger’s The City (1919) to create an abstract FAP mural for Newark Airport that questioned the radical nature of the older generation and rejected the socialist style of Diego Rivera’s murals.12 The FAP, with its fixed weekly salary, offered the young painters of the AAA freedom in their artistic development and engendered in them an increased artistic self-confidence. However, it offered little in the way of exhibition opportunities. George Morris described the genesis of avant-garde art in the spaces that resulted: “it would seem that abstract art can fructify only when the artist remains unhampered as he closes upon the endless problems of form in design.”13 However, the 1935 survey exhibition at the Whitney Museum, Abstract Painting in America, turned out to be a disappointment. As Morris reflected, “most of the artists chosen had become stalled in various ill-digested ferments of impressionism, expressionism, and half-hearted cubism.”14 Meanwhile, for the exhibitions of abstract art at MoMA in 1936–37, the curator Alfred H. Barr relied on European art, that is to say, on established art. The contemporary developments within abstract art by the American avant-garde were disregarded.At roughly the same time, The Ten, another recently established, loose collective, organized a joint exhibition that included Schanker, Bolotowsky, Adolph Gottlieb, and Mark Rothko. This double helix created its own dynamism that enabled the exchange with the Concretionists, a group founded by Gallatin in 1936, and which included other AAA artists such as Charles Biederman, Alexander Calder, Ferren, Morris, and Charles Green Shaw. In this constellation, and despite their independence, The Ten can be seen as the group shaping the format of the AAA. The individualists Graham, Gorky, Davis, and De Kooning, who were reluctant to join any artist groups, defined the spiritual and intellectual climate of a distinctly U.S.-based approach to abstract painting. It was their influence that made it possible for artists in New York to appropriate this new tendency, as Sandler has discussed historically, though they were not part of the group.15By comparison to other groups, the AAA was neither homogeneous nor well organized. However, they were strong competitors on the established art scene and were certainly ambitious. Albers supported them, and André Masson and other important avant-garde artists held presentations for the group. Even the influential French abstract painter Jean Hélion joined the group during his time in New York. The founders also sought to model the group on their European counterparts, such as Abstraction-Création, Cercle et Carré, and Art Concret.16 From 1937 onward, Sophie Taeuber and Jean Arp joined with Morris and Gallatin to publish the journal Plastique.17 These activities intensified the artistic exchange precisely during the year the collective organized its first exhibition, at Squibb Gallery in New York from 3 to 17 April 1937.This was the best-attended exhibition outside a museum that year in New York, clocking up to 1,500 visitors. It was followed by an exhibition at Columbia University from 1 to 30 November the same year, and for the next two years, group exhibitions toured various galleries across the United States, leading Clement Greenberg to state: “The annual exhibitions of the American Abstract Artists … were the most important occasions of these years as far as advanced art in New York was concerned.”18 The self-confidence and the mission of the group’s individual representatives are manifest in the yearbooks of 1938, 1939, and 1946.19 Nevertheless, their attempts to hold their 1938 Annual Exhibition at MoMA failed. Barr had rejected their written requests, arguing that the museum had no available time slot and required approval from the board. This rejection caused frustration in the group.20 Following another historicizing MoMA exhibition, Art in Our Time (1939), and an exhibition of contemporary comic strips, AAA members distributed the provocative protest statement How Modern Is the Museum of Modern Art? outside the museum itself.21 With typography by Ad Reinhardt, this leaflet was a pioneering initiative that demanded MoMA give European and American avant-garde artists greater visibility. MoMA subsequently declared this pamphlet a work of art and added it to their permanent collection.They caused another sensation in 1940 with their critical exhibition in response to the 1939–40 New York World’s Fair. This exhibition included architectural models by Walter Gropius, Marcel Breuer, and Richard Neutra in an attempt to show their broad appeal and present their international reach. However, the more militant AAA activists again sought to vent their dissatisfaction. Rather than producing a yearbook, they published another leaflet titled The Art Critics—!22 In this leaflet, they extended their criticism to include art journalism alongside the art institutions as the official bodies denying them recognition, negating their standing as avant-garde artists, and denigrating the quality of their works. In response, they were defamed by critics as the “American Abstract Academy.” Nevertheless, their renown increased as a result of the controversy. However, with the onset of World War II, the immense appeal of well-known artists emigrating from Europe to escape the conflict, and the rise of new artist associations in New York, their influence quickly waned.Morris, in his introduction to the group’s 1939 yearbook, and probably without intending to do so, laid out the group’s legacy.23 In response to criticism that they were too beholden to the School of Paris, he detailed the continuous development of contemporary art and underscored the need for precursors to engender development: “If art-forms were being realized that would express the contemporary spirit, … which had been the basic properties of art … since the first scratchings of the cave-men … they would have to be put forward by the artists themselves.” He rejects the contemporary argument that abstract art is “un-American” by referring to the past, alluding to both the art of the Ice Age and the prehistoric rock art of North America: “The opposition which abstract art has encountered … in America gives particular cause for surprise in that from the earliest times the native American art was very abstract in feeling.” He underscores that the AAA wants to continue to give people throughout the United States the opportunity to see modern, contemporary American art. Morris recommended to Barr: “An exhibition could be planned so as to include the Stone Age, and various phases of abstract art through … the Arab Periods (when all art was required to be non-representational), … into the contemporary European and American movements.”In their 1946 entry to the AAA yearbook, Albers, Mondrian, and Léger noted the extent to which the historic situation had changed. And Gallatin once again sharply criticized the collection policies of the museum in New York.
